# Real problem

- Who is going to win the election for mayor?
- In the last election, the current mayor got 60% of the votes. Should we assume that's what he'll get this time?
- We can go out and take a survey asking people if they plan to vote for the current mayor again.
- There are many non-statistical problems with this, but we won't dig into those now.
- What do we need to provide a meaningful statistical answer?
- According to Bayes theorem, all we need is a prior belief and a likelihood.

# Core elements
- prior: P( belief )
- posterior: P( belief | data )
- likelihood: P( data | belief )

prior x likelihood -> posterior

# Priors -> Posteriors

- Demonstrate the sequential nature of priors and posteriors, with examples demonstrating common transformations and ask how we can interpret them.

- Priors and posteriors are the same thing. Posteriors become priors for our next observation. This is what updating means.

# Putting priors into practice

- Priors _about what?_ (let's make our definition more specific)
  - "parameters": unknown numerical quantities in the world
  - "estimand": what we want to find out (sometimes a parameter, often a combination of parameters and other info)
- P(belief) -> P(belief about a parameter or parameters)
  - shorthand: P(parameters) or P(Θ)

# Interactive definition of prior
- drag and pull along grid approximation

- Statistics is about randomness. 
- If I flip a coin, I don't know what will happen.
- If I flip a coin 1000 times, I can actually say a lot more.
- Just because we don't know if it will rain tomorrow doesn't mean we don't know anything.
- Probability distributions are they key to everything.

- Dilemma: can't define every value like we did with the stones in the bag
- Introducing grid approximation

# But what is a likelihood?

- Hume vs Gauss example?

- For priors and posteriors, randomness is about our uncertainty, a subjective experience.
- For likelihood, randomness is a property of the world.
- What Hume didn't understand was the idea of a "generating process". Things have probabilities because randomness "comes from somewhere".


# Calculating likelihood

- This is the mathiest thing we're going to talk about together, but you don't ever actually have to do it by hand. We always use software for that. 

- From Bayes theorem, we know that likelihood is: P( data | parameters )
- But what does this mean?

- Given a particular parameter value, how likely is the data we saw.
- This is, not coincidentally, conceptually related to the idea of statistical significance.
- We're treating thing parameter value as fixed, and we're treating the data as probabalistic
- But we do this for every single possible value of our parameter

- If our parameter is _actually_ 50%, what is the probability that we would see a result like 4 / 15 saying they will vote for the mayor.

- If our parameter is _actually_ 30%, what is the probability that we would see a result like 4 / 15 saying they will vote for the mayor.

- If our parameter is _actually_ 80%, what is the probability that we would see a result like 4 / 15 saying they will vote for the mayor.


- The mathematics behind many generating processes is very well understood. A question like, "if I flip a coin 20 times, what is the probability of getting heads exactly 8 times?" is something that we can calculate. Any statistical software (including excel) will be able to tell you.
